newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire diamonds could fuel rebellion.
newsitem.headline: Zaire diamonds could fuel rebellion.

text.p: Diamonds have become the main hard currency earner for embattled Zaire, but they could also help to fuel a rebellion if guerrillas capture one of the main producing districts.
Easily transportable, easily mined diamonds are the one trade that has been able to survive the economic decay and violent crises in what should be one of Africa's richest countries.
Rebels who have taken over a swathe land on the eastern border now say they are headed for Kisangani, Zaire's latest target for diamond fortune-hunters.
In the past few years the stones have given a new lease of life to the moribund eastern river port.
"Business is good or I wouldn't be here," says a Lebanese dealer, known simply as "Ambassadeur".
He was one of those who stuck out the wave of looting that swept the city as soldiers routed by Rwandan-backed rebels retreated 500 km (310 miles) from the eastern frontier.

The rebels have not said they are after diamonds, but are likely to need significant funds both for armaments and to persuade starving, suddenly dislocated people in the region they occupy that they can do better than the previous rulers.
Current insecurity in Kisangani has not stopped the diggers, and the lesson from neighbouring Angola and other war-torn African states rich in diamonds is that almost nothing can.

Angola's rebel UNITA movement used diamond proceeds to finance its 20-year guerrilla war with the government. Rebel groups in other African countries such as Liberia and Sierra Leone have also paid for their wars in part with diamonds.

Officials at the mines ministry said foreign investors, including de Beers, have shown interest in reaching an agreement for mining in Kisangani's Upper Zaire region which is so far the province of fortune-hunters with hand-dug pits.
De Beers' local subsidiary SEDIZA is the biggest single buyer of Zaire's alluvial diamonds, but there is considerable competition from Lebanese and Zairean independent buyers.
Mbuji-Mayi, in central Zaire sprouted from a village into a city which may hold more than a million people solely on the back of its precious stones.
The biggest digger of all is state-run MIBA, Zaire's most profitable firm since the collapse of copper and cobalt mines.

But attention is switching from Mbuji-Mayi as the known haunts are dug out and MIBA's concession comes under increasing threats from night-time trespassers which are only countered by ever better security.

"Things are growing less and less attractive here, not only are the beds being exhausted but everyone knows their diamonds, they all know the value and our profit margins can be very small," said Lebanese community leader and diamond dealer Kamel Ezzeddine.
High quality Angolan gems continue to flood through Zaire, crossing the border from Lunda-Norte province to the towns of Tshikapa and Kahemba.
When the investment required is at most basic a bucket, a shovel, and possibly a water pump it is not hard to see how diamond digging can thrive in Zaire's unstable society.

"Although foreign investors are now showing interest in the copper and cobalt mines at least in the near future diamonds are likely to be the main source of foreign exchange in Zaire," said Luboya Diyoka, director of the business association.
